title: Was Atlantis Founded by Refugees from a Drying Sahara?

content:
​In 1927, the Swedish-American journalist Edwin Björkman published The Search for Atlantis, the first book to my knowledge that argued for the identity of Atlantis and the biblical city of Tarshish, and that both were located near modern Cádiz in southwestern Spain. This claim would recur many times in Atlantis literature, including in the work of Richard Freund in the 2010s, resulting in two documentaries, and again in an unrelated 2025 documentary from a team that claimed to have found the ruins of Atlantis. 

​But one of the first rehashes occurred in 1929 when Ellen Mary Whitshaw, a British expatriate and amateur archaeologist, attempted to prove the claim through her study of folklore in the Andalucia region of Spain, where she had lived for three decades. Where Björkman emphasized the role Cádiz, Whitshaw took a broader regional view and discussed the lore of Niebla, a town some distance north and west. Her hypothesis is that Cádiz, ancient Gades, was the capital of the region of Atlantis ruled by Poseidon’s son Gadir, and the ancient ruins close to Niebla, near to the similarly named Gadea, are a remnant of Atlantis.

My theory, to sum it up concisely, is that Plato’s story is corroborated from first to last by what we find here, even the Atlantean name of his son Gadir, who inherited that part of Poseidon's kingdom which lay beyond the Pillars of Hercules and ruled at Gades, having its echo in the traditional Gadea on the Rio Tinto in the jurisdiction of Niebla, an ancient mill under the shadow of a Stone Age fortress, relics of which still stand.

​The Spectator called her Atlantis in Andalucia: A Study of Folk Memory “a fascinating contribution to the lore of the lost continent,” but in paging through it, one of the stories I found most interesting was the rather unexpected legend of the “Great Drought,” for which Whitshaw provides a most unexpected explanation:

Rodrigo Caro, writing in Sevilla in 1626, quotes a legend that Niebla was the first place to be colonised “after the great drought.” “The few people who survived, fleeing from their devastated country, came to Spain, and seeing trees growing and finding no one to interfere, settled down here” . . . “and so the whole world was populated once more.”

 I take it that this is a folk memory of the drying-up of the once-fertile Sahara in consequence of climatic changes caused by the repeated volcanic disturbances in and around the Atlantean mainland which ended in its final submergence.

 I have not found that legend except in Rodrigo Caro. But here in Niebla we have a flood lore which to the best of my knowledge is unique, and can only, I think, have sprung from the folk memory of great tidal waves created by volcanic action in the Atlantic.

​The idea that a legend like this records the drying of the Sahara is a shocking enough claim, and a very unusual one. Indeed, it seems like the kind of fun argument that we would see on Ancient Aliens and then pick apart with dates and archaeological proof. For instance, the periods of moist and dry Sahara do not align with the timeline of Atlantis, with the most recent period of desertification occurring thousands of years after the time Plato claimed Atlantis fell.

 But, as is so often the case, the author is just lying. I was intrigued enough to look up the claims, and Whitshaw couldn’t have spent much time researching the idea because Caro very clearly says what his sources are.

 Rodrigo Caro was a Spanish priest and antiquarian, who was famous for a poem about Roman ruins but infamous for being taken in by the forged ancient texts of Jerónimo Román de la Higuera, which he edited. In his Antigüedades y principado de la ilustrissima ciudad de Sevilla (1634)—apparently the text Whitshaw ascribes to 1626—Caro is very clear about his source for the story. In Book III, ch. 81, he writes: “The General Estoria of the Lord King Don Alfonso the Wise, in its First Part, says that the town of Niebla was the first place in Spain to be populated after that great drought, which lasted 26 years. It says so in these words…”

 He then goes on to partially quote the relevant passage. Now, the interesting thing is that Alfonso doesn’t say a thing about the Sahara and makes very plain that this is a legend about a drought in Spain and was wholly about Spain. I translate here a larger chunk of Alfonso’s passage, found in the second section of the prologue to the General Estoria, for context. It describes the drought which occurred during the lives of Rocas and Silvio, two brothers associated with the founding of Toledo:

Until such time as the great drought came, which lasted twenty-six years, during which it did not rain in Spain. Because of this, all the people of the land had to flee, and those two brothers died. There was not a river in all Spain that did not dry up, except the Guadalquivir and the Ebro, and these flowed very little. The entire land was ruined and desolate, and nothing remained in it. All the people crossed the Pyrenees mountains, which are the passes of Aspa, and went to seek refuge in other lands. Throughout the country they composed songs of lamentation for Spain, saying that God had become angry with it. And it happened that in the final year of the drought there arose such a great wind that it uprooted all the trees, finding them dry. So much dust did the wind raise that it looked like smoke, and people thought the whole land was burning. Then three years followed in which nothing happened but rain, so that the entire land was covered with water, resembling a sea, and everything that had been lost began to recover. And the people who were natives of the land, although they had settled elsewhere, could not bear to remain away. As soon as they learned that the land was improving, they returned to Spain. They found no green trees anywhere in the country except for a very few along the banks of the Guadalquivir and Ebro, and these were olive trees or pomegranates. They began to repopulate the places that had been inhabited before. And because they said that the calamity that had come upon Spain was like a plague, the first town they newly repopulated was between the western sea and the Guadalquivir River. They gave it the name Lepra, which today they call Niebla.

As you can see, Whitshaw selectively extracted words from Caro and Alfonso to create a false narrative, omitting the context that the Spaniards fled the drought in Spain before returning to reestablish civilization. Instead, she has rewritten the text to make it into a migration story from the drying Sahara to Spain as part of her imaginary vision of the mythic foundation of Atlantis. Now, part of this is forgivable—Caro had omitted the earlier part of Alfonso’s narrative, so Whitshaw would not have known the story started in Spain from Caro alone. But the other half is not forgivable since Caro very clearly told her exactly where to find the story, and Alfonso’s text had been edited and published in 1906 and was widely available in Spanish libraries when Whitshaw researched her own book in 1929.

 And just as a bonus, Caro said Alfonso’s story is also given in Alvar Gutiérrez de Torres’s El sumario de las maravillosas y espantables cosas que en el mundo han acontescido (1524), where, indeed, it appears nearly verbatim. Whitshaw missed that, too.
